title: Advanced Next.js — Server Actions, Streaming, and the Edge

subChunks.title: Advanced Next.js — Server Actions, Streaming, and the Edge
subChunks.hookHtml: Next.js App Router introduced patterns that blur the line between frontend and backend: Server Actions let you write server-side mutations directly in React components. Streaming sends HTML progressively to the browser. Edge runtime moves computation closer to users. These are the patterns that make Next.js applications genuinely full-stack.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Server Actions — mutations from the server

// app/quests/actions.ts
'use server';
import { db } from '@/lib/db';
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';

export async function acceptQuest(questId: number) {
  // This runs on the server — has DB access, no API route needed:
  await db.quest.update({
    where: { id: questId },
    data: { status: 'accepted' },
  });

  // Revalidate the cache so the page shows fresh data:
  revalidatePath('/quests');
}

// In a Client Component:
'use client';
import { acceptQuest } from './actions';

export function AcceptButton({ questId }: { questId: number }) {
  return (
    <form action={acceptQuest.bind(null, questId)}>
      <button type="submit">Accept Quest</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Progressive enhancement with Server Actions

// Server Actions work without JavaScript — the form submits natively:
// When JS loads, React enhances it to submit without page reload

import { useFormStatus, useFormState } from 'react-dom';

function SubmitButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();
  return <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>{pending ? 'Saving...' : 'Save'}</button>
}

async function submitAction(prevState: any, formData: FormData) {
  'use server';
  const title = formData.get('title') as string;
  if (!title) return { error: 'Title is required' };
  await db.quest.create({ data: { title } });
  revalidatePath('/quests');
  return { success: true };
}

function QuestForm() {
  const [state, action] = useFormState(submitAction, {});
  return (
    <form action={action}>
      <input name="title" />
      {state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
      <SubmitButton />
    </form>
  );
}

Streaming with Suspense

// app/dashboard/page.tsx:
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { QuestList } from './QuestList';
import { MemberStats } from './MemberStats';
import { TreasuryChart } from './TreasuryChart';

// These three components fetch data independently
// HTML streams to the browser as each resolves:
export default function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Suspense fallback={<QuestListSkeleton />}>
        <QuestList />  {/* Fast — streams first */}
      </Suspense>
      <Suspense fallback={<StatsSkeleton />}>
        <MemberStats />  {/* Medium — streams second */}
      </Suspense>
      <Suspense fallback={<ChartSkeleton />}>
        <TreasuryChart />  {/* Slow — streams last */}
      </Suspense>
    </div>
  );
}

Edge Runtime

// app/api/auth/route.ts — runs at the CDN edge:
export const runtime = 'edge';

export async function GET(request: Request) {
  // Runs in ~50ms worldwide instead of ~200ms from a single region
  const token = request.headers.get('authorization');
  // JWT verification, geo-routing, A/B testing...
  return Response.json({ valid: !!token });
}

// Middleware.ts — runs on every request at the edge:
export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  const token = request.cookies.get('auth-token');
  if (!token && request.nextUrl.pathname.startsWith('/dashboard')) {
    return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url));
  }
}

Vex: "Server Actions remove the API layer for mutations. revalidatePath removes the cache invalidation layer. Streaming removes the waterfall — the page starts loading before all data is ready. The Edge moves computation to the user. Each of these is an architectural choice with trade-offs — not features to use by default."

storyBeats.text: An admin form. A Server Action. No API route. The mutation runs on the server, the cache invalidates, the page reflects the change — all from inside the React component. The architecture has collapsed the stack.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Server Actions collapse the API layer for simple mutations. Streaming collapses the loading waterfall — send HTML for fast sections first, stream slow sections after. The Edge collapses geographic latency — auth middleware runs 50ms from the user instead of 200ms from a single region.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: But: Server Actions are not a replacement for an API if you have mobile clients, third-party integrations, or need versioned endpoints. Streaming adds complexity to loading state design. The Edge runtime has a limited API surface — no native Node.js APIs. Know the trade-offs before you choose.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Architecture exercise — Server Actions and Streaming:

  • Write a Server Action that creates a quest (takes FormData, validates title, creates in DB, revalidates /quests path)
  • Write the client form that uses it with useFormStatus for pending state
  • Write a dashboard page that streams three independent data sections using Suspense with skeleton fallbacks
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a complete Next.js App Router form with full progressive enhancement: a quest creation form that (1) works without JavaScript using a Server Action bound to a native HTML form, (2) enhances with React when JS loads (useFormStatus for pending state, useFormState for error display), (3) uses Zod for server-side validation within the Server Action, and (4) redirects to the quest detail page on success. Test by disabling JavaScript in DevTools and verifying the form still submits.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Server Actions — what layer of the traditional React architecture do they replace, and what are their limits? Explain streaming with Suspense — what is sent to the browser first, and how does it differ from loading all data before sending HTML? Explain Edge runtime — what is it, what can't it do, and why is it valuable for auth middleware?

questions.prompt: What does `revalidatePath('/quests')` do inside a Server Action?
options: Invalidates Next.js's full-route cache for /quests — on the next request, the page will be re-rendered with fresh data instead of serving a cached version
Redirects the user to /quests after the action completes
Clears the client-side TanStack Query cache for queries containing 'quests'
questions.answer: Invalidates Next.js's full-route cache for /quests — on the next request, the page will be re-rendered with fresh data instead of serving a cached version
questions.explanation: Next.js aggressively caches page renders. After a mutation (creating, updating, deleting data), the cached version is stale. revalidatePath('/quests') marks that cached entry as stale — the next request to /quests will re-render the Server Component and fetch fresh data. Without this, users would see stale data after their mutation. revalidateTag() does the same for named cache tags.

questions.prompt: When should you use Server Actions vs a traditional REST API endpoint for mutations in Next.js?
options: Server Actions for mutations only consumed by this Next.js app. REST API for mutations that need to be consumed by mobile clients, external services, or third-party integrations.
Always Server Actions — they eliminate the need for any API layer
REST API for all mutations — Server Actions are only for static sites
Server Actions for read operations, REST API for writes
questions.answer: Server Actions for mutations only consumed by this Next.js app. REST API for mutations that need to be consumed by mobile clients, external services, or third-party integrations.
questions.explanation: Server Actions are tightly coupled to Next.js — they're called via a special POST request format, not a standard REST endpoint. If a React Native app or third-party webhook needs to call the same mutation, a REST endpoint is necessary. Server Actions excel for web-only mutations: form submissions, cart updates, admin actions where the caller is always your Next.js UI.
